relationship: concentrate users reached substantially higher plasma THC than flower users; significant main effect of form and a significant form-by-time(quadratic) interaction
magnitude_note: Point estimates and model SEs are given directly in Table 2. Note a labeling discrepancy: Abstract/Discussion separately restate these same means with variability figures (0.43 for concentrate, 0.16 for flower) labeled 'SE' in the Abstract and 'SD' in the Discussion — see studies.json data_ambiguity_flags for bidwell-2020. That population-level SD/SE is NOT the same number as Table 2's smaller model-based SE quoted above; both are preserved, unreconciled, rather than picking one.

variable: self-reported intoxication (avg. of feeling high/mentally stoned/physically stoned)
relationship: despite ~2.3x higher plasma THC in concentrate users, peak subjective intoxication did NOT differ significantly between flower and concentrate users (main effect of form not significant) -- the study's central Potency =/= Impairment finding
claim_status_note: The headline claim (no overall form difference in peak intoxication) is supported by the non-significant main effect. But do not oversimplify to 'completely identical': the form-by-linear-time interaction IS significant (p=.01), meaning the two groups' intoxication trajectories over the session differ in shape even though their overall levels don't separate. This nuance is exactly the kind of thing the evidence-visualization product should surface rather than flatten.
source_ref: Table 2; Results 'Subjective Drug Effects' (H2-12); Abstract 'Key Points > Findings'

relationship: concentrate users reported LOWER tension and LOWER vigor than flower users across all assessments -- a form effect in the opposite direction from what a simple 'more potent = more intense' model would predict
magnitude_note: Flagged as a counterintuitive/contradiction-worthy finding per the Deep Research brief's instruction to treat contradiction as a product feature: this is a case where a form effect on subjective state DOES exist, but points opposite to what higher blood THC in concentrate users would predict.

variable: delayed verbal recall errors (shopping list task)
relationship: errors increased after cannabis use in both flower and concentrate users; no significant difference by form or by potency -- impairment occurs but does not track the proxy chain
magnitude_note: This is the abstract's headline cognitive-impairment statistic (F(1,203)=32.31, P<.001), cited verbatim.

relationship: sway increased short-term post-use (~11% increase per Discussion) then recovered to baseline by 1 hour, in both flower and concentrate users; no significant difference by form
magnitude_note: This is the abstract's headline balance statistic (F(1,203)=18.88, P<.001), cited verbatim. Authors note this magnitude is comparable to balance effects reported for 0.05-0.10% blood alcohol concentration, and propose balance as a candidate field-sobriety-style marker of recent use.

variable: plasma THC by potency subgroup (16% vs 24% flower; 70% vs 90% concentrate)
relationship: no significant within-form association between labeled THC potency and blood THC levels -- i.e. 16% vs 24% flower did not produce significantly different blood THC, nor did 70% vs 90% concentrate

significance.overall: text states 'no within-form association of THC potency with blood levels'; no F/p values or means given for the potency subgroup comparison itself in the main text (see Supplement 2 eResults / eTable 1 / eTable 2, not yet retrieved)

claim_status_note: Supported as a reported null result, but the underlying subgroup statistics live in a supplementary file (jamapsychiatry-77-787-s001.pdf, Supplement 2) that has not yet been fetched -- treat the numeric strength of this null as unconfirmed until that supplement is retrieved.
magnitude_note: This is the exact evidentiary basis for the product's rule against fabricating separate 16%-vs-24%-flower or 70%-vs-90%-concentrate plasma values: the source itself only reports non-significance, not the subgroup means.
source_ref: Discussion (H1-4); Supplement 2 (eResults, eTable 1, eTable 2) -- not yet retrieved

variable: blood/oral-fluid THC biomarkers and subjective intoxication vs driving/cognitive impairment (Other/occasional cannabis users, inhaled route)
relationship: higher biomarker concentrations and subjective intoxication ARE significantly associated with greater impairment in occasional users after inhaling THC, but the relationships are only very-weak to moderate in strength -- direction is as expected, magnitude is not clinically reassuring as a threshold

values.strength_band: moderate -- the strongest relationship found in the whole analysis, from a non-intoxicating metabolite

significance.note: Each analysis (except blood THC post-inhalation) carried a significant amount of residual heterogeneity, and the unmoderated versions of the 11-OH-THC/11-COOH-THC analyses showed high homogeneity -- making it hard to isolate the influence of any one covariate. Authors flag this as a genuine limitation on the analyses' robustness, not just a caveat.

magnitude_note: R-values and CIs taken verbatim from Results 3.2.1 prose (cross-checked against the Abstract's restatement of the same numbers). The full per-domain regression coefficient table (Table 3) was not reliably extractable from OCR'd text -- see studies.json data_completeness_note.

variable: blood THC biomarkers and subjective intoxication vs driving/cognitive impairment (Regular/weekly-or-more cannabis users, inhaled route)
relationship: NO significant relationship between any THC biomarker (or subjective intoxication) and impairment in regular cannabis users -- this is the study's central 'Blood THC =/= Cannabis BAC' finding, since it means the same blood concentration that predicts (weakly) in occasional users predicts nothing in regular users

significance.note: p's>0.10 for all. Authors explicitly caveat that these regular-user analyses are 'less robust' than the occasional-user analyses (smaller samples; the unmoderated versions showed high homogeneity, again limiting ability to isolate covariate influence). No eligible studies measured oral-route THC or oral-fluid THC in regular users at all -- those cells are structurally empty, not non-significant.

claim_status_note: The null result itself is supported by the reported statistics, but authors explicitly flag it as resting on a less robust evidence base than the occasional-user findings -- 'caution is advised.' Treat 'no relationship' as 'no relationship detected with the available data,' not as proof of true independence.

variable: scale/composition of the underlying evidence base
relationship: 28 publications, 824 participants (71% male), 57 trials, 822 eligible outcome instances feeding the meta-regression; mean study-quality (Rosendal) score 70% (SD 10%, range 53-93%)
source_ref: Results 3.1 'Overview of included studies and study quality'; Abstract
